This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building time series — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary time series tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Before starting time series work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
2. Document any non-obvious time series decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
3. When time series guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
4. Surface known limitations of a chosen time series approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
5. Re-check edge cases relevant to time series (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
6. When time series decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
7. When multiple time series strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
8. Check that time series terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
9. Validate time series outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid mixing unrelated time series concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not skip documenting time series assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not apply generic time series advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Avoid introducing new time series abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not silently drop time series edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.

CLOSING NOTE
When in doubt, prefer clarity and explicit reasoning about time series over a shortcut that saves a few lines but hides intent.
